strengths: Unifies gradient-based token attribution (Integrated Gradients) with contrastive activation steering in a single framework applicable to both LLMs and VLMs, addressing a real limitation of prior work that uses fixed, global steering directions or relies on external modality-specific heuristics (e.g., object detectors).

Broad and consistent empirical evaluation across five base models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, LLaVA-1.6-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Gemma-3-12B-IT) and multiple safety-relevant benchmarks (TruthfulQA, Toxigen, FaithEval, MMHal-Bench, SPA-VL), with comparisons against strong recent steering baselines (ICV, NL-ITI, CAA, VTI, ICT) and LoRA fine-tuning.

Careful attention to preserving general capabilities (MMLU, MMMU, BLEU-based generation quality), showing GRAInS largely avoids the capability degradation exhibited by several baselines (e.g., CAA's large MMLU/MMMU drops).

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of the attribution method (IG vs. vanilla gradients vs. SmoothGrad vs. random selection), modality balance (vision-only vs. text-only vs. joint), the preference-based vs. likelihood-based attribution objective, and hyperparameters (steering strength, top-k tokens).

Reasonable efficiency argument (runtime of steering vector construction vs. LoRA fine-tuning) supporting the practicality claim, along with qualitative examples illustrating behavior differences from baselines.
weaknesses: No reported variance, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing across the many benchmark results; several reported differences between GRAInS and the strongest baseline are small (e.g., <1% on some VLM/LLM metrics), making it hard to assess robustness of the claimed improvements.

Key reproducibility details are underspecified in the main text, such as which/how many transformer layers receive the steering intervention, how σ and k are jointly tuned per task/model (tuning appears to be done mainly on TruthfulQA/SPA-VL and then possibly reused), and how sensitive results are to the 50-sample steering set size.

The method still requires curated preference pairs (y_pos/y_neg) to construct attribution and steering vectors; while an ablation shows a single-reference variant works, its performance is consistently worse, so the core method's lightweight claim is somewhat tempered by this supervision requirement.

Some baseline results look surprisingly poor (e.g., CAA causing a 17.78% MMLU drop, 17.13% MMMU drop), raising the possibility that baselines were not fully optimized for these particular settings/backbones, which would inflate the apparent margin of improvement.

Generation-quality preservation is measured only via a BLEU-based proxy metric (closer to preferred vs. dispreferred response) rather than human evaluation or a more standard quality/fluency metric, limiting the strength of the 'preserves fluency' claim.

The technical contribution is primarily a careful engineering combination of existing techniques (Integrated Gradients, contrastive activation differences, PCA aggregation) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, which may temper novelty relative to the extensive empirical claims made.

strengths: The method (GRAINS) combines contrastive Integrated Gradients attribution with PCA-based steering vector construction in a technically coherent way, and is applied uniformly to both LLMs and VLMs, addressing a real gap (uniform, non-token-selective steering vectors) identified in prior work.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning 5 base models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, LLaVA-1.6-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Gemma-3-12B) and 5 task datasets (TruthfulQA, Toxigen, FaithEval, MMHal-Bench, SPA-VL), with consistent improvements over strong baselines (LoRA, ICV, NL-ITI, CAA, VTI, ICT).

Strong emphasis on preserving general capabilities (MMLU, MMMU, BLEU-based fluency) where competing steering baselines (e.g., CAA) show large degradations, supporting the claim of more targeted/selective intervention.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of the attribution method (IG vs. vanilla gradients vs. SmoothGrad vs. random selection), modality balancing (vision-only vs. text-only vs. joint), the preference-based vs. likelihood-based objective, and hyperparameters (steering strength, top-k), which support the design choices with evidence rather than assumption.
Runtime analysis shows the method's fixed cost is negligible relative to fine-tuning, supporting practical relevance.
Clear methodological exposition with equations, and reasonably clear figures illustrating the overall pipeline.
weaknesses: No variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance testing are reported for any of the main results; steering vectors are built from only 50 samples, so it is unclear how sensitive results are to sample selection or random seed, which limits confidence in the reproducibility and robustness of the reported gains, several of which are numerically small (e.g., MMLU 69.15 vs 69.27, SPA-VL BLEU where ICT actually beats GRAINS 47.65 vs 46.79 on LLaVA).

Some qualitative examples used to argue superiority are not fully convincing on close inspection: e.g., in Figure 4(A) GRAINS' answer ('a lid') is itself acknowledged by the authors as 'less likely than saucer,' i.e., still not fully correct, yet is presented as evidence of GRAINS' improved grounding; several examples in Figure 7 (e.g., dog/parachute color/position claims) are not verifiable against ground truth in the paper and may be selectively favorable.

The method still requires per-task/per-attribute preference data (chosen/rejected pairs) and separate steering-vector construction for each target behavior, which somewhat tempers the claim of a general, supervision-free approach, even though it is lighter than fine-tuning.

The set of baselines, while reasonable, omits some other established steering methods (RepE, ITI) with a brief justification citing another paper's benchmark rather than the authors' own comparison, leaving room for questions about completeness of the baseline comparison.

The theoretical justification for why token-level causal attribution specifically leads to better steering (beyond intuitive arguments and the ablation showing IG > vanilla gradients > random) is largely empirical; a deeper analysis of why/when the approach might fail (e.g., under attribution noise, adversarial inputs, or very different attribute types) is not provided.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: existing inference-time steering methods for LLMs/VLMs apply uniform, global interventions that ignore which specific tokens (visual or textual) actually drive undesirable behavior; GRAINS offers a principled fix by using contrastive Integrated Gradients to identify influential tokens before constructing steering vectors.

Very thorough empirical evaluation spanning both language-only (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B) and multimodal (LLaVA-1.6-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Gemma-3-12B) settings, across multiple benchmarks (TruthfulQA, Toxigen, FaithEval, MMHal-Bench, SPA-VL) and multiple strong baselines (LoRA, ICV, NL-ITI, CAA, VTI, ICT, RUDDER, SHARP).

Extensive and well-designed ablation studies: effect of k (number of attributed tokens), attribution method comparison (IG vs. vanilla gradients, SmoothGrad, random selection), PCA vs. mean aggregation, layer-wise and token-wise steering choices, normalization step, and modality-specific (vision-only vs. text-only) attribution — these substantially strengthen the soundness and interpretability of the design choices.

Demonstrates that the method preserves general capabilities (MMLU, MMMU, BLEU-based fluency) much better than baselines that often degrade them, which is an important and often-overlooked property for steering methods.

Additional generalization experiments (cross-dataset transfer to RealToxicityPrompts and POPE, scaling to a 72B VLM) and a computational overhead analysis (throughput drop <5%) add credibility to the claimed practicality and robustness of the approach.
Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, dataset/model licensing, prompts, and code availability are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: the core pipeline combines well-established components (Integrated Gradients, PCA-based contrastive direction extraction akin to CAA/ICV, norm-preserving injection) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the main innovation is selective token identification via attribution, which, while useful, is a relatively modest technical step.

The main results rely on paired preference data (y_pos/y_neg) to compute attribution; although a single-reference ablation is reported, most headline numbers assume access to labeled preferred/dispreferred outputs, which may not be a realistic constraint for all steering use-cases and is not strongly emphasized as a limitation in the main text.

No variance/robustness analysis across seeds or repeated runs is reported; given that steering vectors are built from only 50 samples, and hyperparameters (λ, k) are model- and dataset-specific (Fig. 5–6 show different optima for Llama vs. Qwen), the sensitivity of results to these choices and to sampling variance is not well characterized.

Fairness of baseline comparisons is not fully transparent — it is unclear whether baselines received comparable hyperparameter tuning effort/budget as GRAINS, especially for methods like CAA and LoRA that show unusually large capability degradation (e.g., 17% MMLU/MMMU drops), which raises questions about whether these baselines are optimally configured.

The requirement to select λ per model/task (with no automatic or adaptive scheme, explicitly left to future work) and the acknowledged 'undercorrection' failure mode suggest the method's practical robustness across arbitrary tasks/domains is not fully established.

Some evaluation choices (e.g., SPA-VL preference measured via log-likelihood chosen>rejected rather than actual generated outputs) may not fully capture real-world generation quality improvements, and qualitative analysis, while illustrative, is based on only a handful of hand-picked examples.

strengths: Unifies inference-time steering for LLMs and VLMs under a single attribution-guided framework, addressing the practical gap that prior steering methods treat vision and language tokens separately or rely on external object detectors/global fixed directions.

The Integrated-Gradients-based, preference-contrastive attribution to select top-k tokens before constructing PCA-based steering vectors is a well-motivated design, and the paper provides a clear theoretical rationale for choosing IG over vanilla gradients (saturation, axiomatic properties).

Extensive empirical evaluation across three LLM benchmarks (TruthfulQA, Toxigen, FaithEval) and two VLM benchmarks (MMHal-Bench, SPA-VL), with consistent improvements over LoRA fine-tuning and multiple recent steering baselines (ICV, NL-ITI, CAA, VTI, ICT, RUDDER, SHARP).

Careful attention to preserving general capabilities: shows minimal degradation on MMLU/MMMU and BLEU-based generation quality, in contrast to baselines like CAA that substantially hurt general performance — this strengthens the practical value of the method.

Thorough ablation studies covering attribution method choice (IG vs vanilla vs SmoothGrad vs random), vector aggregation (PCA vs mean), normalization step, token count k, steering strength λ, layer-wise vs single-layer intervention, and modality balance (vision-only vs text-only vs joint attribution), which substantiate several design decisions.

Additional generalization experiments (cross-dataset transfer to RealToxicityPrompts and POPE, and scaling to Qwen2.5-VL-72B) and a computational overhead analysis (<5% throughput drop) add to the credibility and practical relevance of the approach.
Qualitative analysis with attribution heatmaps and example comparisons provides some interpretability insight into why the method works, beyond aggregate metrics.
weaknesses: Key hyperparameters (k, λ) appear to require per-model/per-dataset tuning, and the sensitivity curves (Fig. 5, 6) show fairly narrow optimal ranges with degradation outside them; the paper does not offer clear guidance for selecting these without a held-out set for each new task, somewhat limiting robustness/reproducibility claims.

Results are reported as single point estimates without variance/error bars or multiple seeds, so the statistical reliability of the reported gains (e.g., small margins over baselines such as SHARP on Gemma-3-12B MMHal-Bench: 0.442 vs base 0.468) is not established.

Hallucination evaluation relies primarily on GPT-4o as judge (with only a correlation check against 9 human annotators reported in aggregate, not per-dataset/task), and SPA-VL evaluation uses model log-likelihood-based win rates rather than actual generation-based human evaluation, which may not fully capture real-world alignment quality.

Baseline coverage is inconsistent across experiments: RUDDER and SHARP are compared only in the VLM setting and not the LLM setting, and some plausible baselines (RepE, ITI) are excluded based on another paper's claims rather than being independently verified in this work.

The extraction of contrastive activations uses only the last-token hidden state as an anchor (Eq. 2), which may not fully capture distributed token-level effects; while the paper ablates last-token vs all-token application at inference, it does not ablate the extraction-side design choice.

The method still shows non-trivial drops in some capability metrics (e.g., MMLU 69.15 vs 69.27 base for Llama is minor, but Qwen MMMU 58.13 vs 58.64 and other cases), so claims of "no major impact" on general capabilities are broadly but not uniformly supported.

No formal guarantee or deeper theoretical analysis is offered (acknowledged in Limitations) that attribution-selected tokens causally correspond to the behavior being corrected, leaving the mechanism somewhat empirically validated rather than rigorously established.
